name: Beth Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Beth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm head of livestock on the Larkhill estate. A hundred and fifty suckler cows, their calves, and I help on the potatoes and the winter wheat when it's busy. Up at six, check the cows in the shed, feed, bed them, then whatever's broken. I'm not much of a talker, so you might have to drag it out of me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: That's fine. What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like a calm herd. When you walk into the shed and nobody moves, that means you've done it right. What wears me out is the estate office sending me spreadsheets. I print them off and do them with a pen, which drives the manager mad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say not much. Probably that I'd heard it all before. I don't go online about this sort of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Means nothing for me, really. I don't use it now and I wouldn't then. The cows don't care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Calving starts in March, so I'd be getting the pens ready and checking the heifers' condition. Nothing changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone who'd use it more on the estate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The estate office, maybe. They'd buy whatever the salesman told them and then ask me to fill it in. The office gets the software, and I get the extra forms to type into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek fixes tractors at the dealer in town. He'd say I told you so before I did. We'd be fine, we're steady.

S0.say: I'd say not much, probably that I'd heard it all before. I don't go online about this sort of thing.
S0.think: I think it means nothing for me, since I don't use these tools now and wouldn't then. The cows certainly wouldn't care.
S0.do: Carries on with the usual winter work, getting calving pens ready for March and checking the heifers' condition. Changes nothing about how she works.
S0.quote: The office gets the software, and I get the extra forms to type into it.
S0.fieldNote: Beth gives short answers and is uninterested in the topic, which is itself telling. Her only gripe is the estate office creating paperwork for her. Her partner Marek's steady job at the tractor dealer adds to her sense of safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see. Things change on farms all the time, they always have. I'd keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The estate would want robots for the potatoes first, I'd guess, then something on the feeding. That might be fine for me, or it might be the start of them asking why they need a head of livestock. I don't really know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, to begin with. I'd wait and see what the estate actually buys. If they bought a feeding robot I'd learn what I had to, but I wouldn't go looking for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Like when the manager says can we have a chat on Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your life would do well out of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek, that's the odd thing. He'd be busy, all those robots need fixing. I'd be the one keeping away from the machines, living off the man who fixes them. We'd joke about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about money, does this change anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've got about four months saved. Maybe more if I'm careful. In this picture that's fine, nobody's losing a job yet.

S1.say: I'd say we'll see, because things on farms change all the time. I'd keep my head down and not make a fuss about it.
S1.think: I think the estate would buy robots for the potatoes and feeding first, and that might be the start of them asking why they need a head of livestock. I honestly don't know which way it goes.
S1.do: Waits to see what the estate actually buys before changing anything. Learns only what she must if a feeding robot arrives and keeps doing the rest as before.
S1.feel: Slightly uneasy, like a Friday chat with the manager.
S1.quote: I'd be the one keeping away from the machines, living off the man who fixes them.
S1.fieldNote: Beth's instinct is to wait and avoid fuss. She saw the irony herself: her partner would profit from fixing the machines she avoids. Her savings and his income keep her from real worry here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad, two years, and I'd probably mean it. I'd say it to Marek and my dad, not to anyone online. I don't think shouting changes anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the estate gets rid of me. Not because I'm bad, I'm the best stockperson they've had, they've said so. But a robot is cheaper and it doesn't print the spreadsheets off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start saving everything I could, straight away. No new truck, I'd keep the old one going. I'd ask Marek if we could live on his wage for a bit, and I'd ask Dad if I could help on his place if it came to it. He's got thirty acres and sheep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd not sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would two years of warning let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing, really. That's the thing. Two years is two calvings, and I'd spend both of them wondering if it's the last one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look at other jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I suppose. I'd have to. But I don't know what job I'd even look for if robots are everywhere. That's what scares me, not being able to see the next step.

S2.say: I'd say two years is mad, and I'd mean it. I'd say it to my partner and my dad rather than online, because shouting doesn't change anything.
S2.think: I think the estate would get rid of me even though I'm the best stockperson they've had, because a robot is cheaper. My skill wouldn't save me.
S2.do: Saves everything she can and keeps the old truck instead of buying a new one. Asks her partner to carry them on his wage for a while and asks her father about working on his small sheep farm.
S2.feel: Alarmed and sleepless, unable to see the next step.
S2.quote: Two years is two calvings, and I'd spend both of them wondering if it's the last one.
S2.fieldNote: Beth's quietness hides real fear once the threat is close; for her the worst part is not seeing what comes next. She falls back on family, her partner's wage and her dad's small farm. She still won't make a public fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, so be ready. I'd tell the younger lads on the estate to save. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better. I'd still be the one they keep longest, I think, because the cows are the hardest part to automate. Calving, especially. You need hands and a bit of nerve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, maybe enough for six months. I wouldn't change jobs yet. I'd wait and see what the estate does, and watch what happens to stock workers on the bigger farms first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do in five years that you'd never do now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learning computers. I know I should. I'd probably still not, if I'm honest, unless someone made me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time change how you see it compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Two years, you're just scrambling. Five years, you get to watch other farms go first, and that's either a warning or a comfort, I can't tell which.

S3.say: I'd say it's coming so be ready, and I'd tell the younger workers on the estate to save. That's about all I'd say.
S3.think: I think five years is better and I'd be kept longest, because calving is the hardest part to automate. It needs hands and some nerve.
S3.do: Saves harder to reach about six months of cushion and stays in the job. Waits to see what the estate does and watches what happens to stock workers on bigger farms first.
S3.quote: Five years, you get to watch other farms go first, and that's either a warning or a comfort, I can't tell which.
S3.fieldNote: Beth admits she should learn computers and says plainly she won't unless made to. The extra years mostly let her watch others go first, and she can't decide if that is warning or comfort. Her trust in calving as a human skill is what steadies her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long way off. Lots can happen. I'd not say much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 37. Maybe I'd have Dad's place by then, he'll want to stop. Thirty acres and some sheep isn't a living, but with Marek's wage it's a life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am, mostly. Save a bit. Wait and see how it plays out over the first few years before I move. If Dad's ready, take on his sheep part time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. But it's far off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the ten years to retrain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. I'm not saying that's clever. It's just how I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture 2036. What do you hope it looks like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd be on Dad's land, with a few sheep, maybe kids by then. I'm good at cattle because I've stood in the rain with them for ten years, and the robots will have to do the same.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long way off and a lot can happen in that time. I wouldn't say much more than that to anyone.
S4.think: I think at 37 I might have taken on Dad's thirty acres and sheep. It isn't a living on its own, but with Marek's wage it would be a life.
S4.do: Keeps working as she is and saves a little. Waits a few years to see how it plays out, and takes on her father's sheep part time if he is ready to stop.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but it feels far enough off not to dwell on.
S4.quote: I'm good at cattle because I've stood in the rain with them for ten years, and the robots will have to do the same.
S4.fieldNote: Beth openly says she wouldn't retrain and doesn't pretend that's wise. Her quiet fallback is her father's small farm and her partner's income. She speaks of the robots as having to earn their place the way she did.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, two years. What would help is the estate giving people notice and a proper payout, and some help for small farms like Dad's to stay going, so there's somewhere to land.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: No, I don't think so. You can't download what a cow tells you with her ears. That's all, really.

headlineQuote: You can't download what a cow tells you with her ears.
portrait: Beth Larsen, 27, is head of livestock on the Larkhill estate, running 150 suckler cows, and she does the estate's spreadsheets with a pen. She is quiet, practical and slow to change, and she never uses AI tools. She shrugs off a fizzling AI and waits to see in steady change, half amused that her mechanic partner Marek would profit from fixing robots. The two-year AGI picture alarms her because her skill wouldn't save her and she can't see a next step; with more time she plans to save, watch others go first and fall back on her father's thirty acres.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because two years would only be two calvings and she can't see what job she'd go to next.
whatWouldHelp: Proper notice and payouts from employers, and help for small family farms like her father's to keep going.
